Solution and Asymptotic Behavior for a Nonlocal Coupled System of Reaction-DiffusionThanks: UFPA, Rua Augusto Corrêa 01, CEP 66075-110, Pará, Brazil. ducival@oi.com.br

Carlos Alberto Raposo ††thanks: UFSJ, Praça Frei Orlando 170, Cep 36307-352, São João del-Rei, MG, Brasil. raposo@ufsj.edu.br    Mauricio Sepúlveda ††thanks: Departamento de Ingeniería Matemática, Universidad de Concepción, Casilla 160-C, Concepción, Chile. mauricio@ing-mat.udec.cl    Octavio Vera Villagrán ††thanks: Departamento de Matemática, Universidad del Bío-Bío, Collao 1202, Casilla 5-C, Concepción, Chile. overa@ubiobio.cl Affiliation: Ducival Carvallo Pereira    Mauro Lima Santos ††thanks: UFPA, Rua Augusto Corrêa 01, CEP 66075-110, Pará, Brazil. ls@ufpa.br
Abstract

This paper concerns with existence, uniqueness and asymptotic behavior of the solutions for a nonlocal coupled system of reaction-diffusion. We prove the existence and uniqueness of weak solutions by the Faedo-Galerkin method and exponential decay of solutions by the classic energy method. We improve the results obtained by Chipot-Lovato and Menezes for coupled systems. A numerical scheme is presented.

Keywords and phrases: Coupled system of reaction-diffusion, The Faedo-Galerkin method, Asymptotic Behavior, Numerical Methods.
Mathematics Subject Classification: 35K57, 35B35

1 Introduction

We consider the reaction-diffusion coupled system in parallel way via parameter α>0\alpha>0 of the form

ut−a⁡(l⁡(u))​Δ​u+f⁡(u−v)\displaystyle u_{t}-a(l(u))\,\Delta u+f(u-v) =\displaystyle= α⁡(u−v)inΩ×(0,T)\displaystyle\alpha\,(u-v)\quad\mbox{in}\quad\Omega\times(0,\,T) (1.1)
vt−a⁡(l⁡(v))​Δ​v−f⁡(u−v)\displaystyle v_{t}-a(l(v))\,\Delta v-f(u-v) =\displaystyle= α⁡(v−u)inΩ×(0,T)\displaystyle\alpha\,(v-u)\quad\mbox{in}\quad\Omega\times(0,\,T) (1.2)
u=v\displaystyle u=v =\displaystyle= 0in∂Ω×(0,T)\displaystyle 0\quad\mbox{in}\quad\partial\Omega\times(0,\,T) (1.3)
u⁡(x, 0)\displaystyle u(x,\,0) =\displaystyle= u0​(x)inΩ\displaystyle u_{0}(x)\quad\mbox{in}\quad\Omega (1.4)
v⁡(x, 0)\displaystyle v(x,\,0) =\displaystyle= v0​(x)inΩ\displaystyle v_{0}(x)\quad\mbox{in}\quad\Omega (1.5)

where u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,\,t) and v=v⁡(x,t)v=v(x,\,t) are real valued functions. Ω\Omega is a bounded domain of ℝn,\mathbb{R}^{n}, ∂Ω\partial\Omega is the boundary of Ω\Omega of class C2.C^{2}. f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} and a:ℝ→ℝa:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} are Lipschitz continuous functions with a⁡(ξ)≥m>0.a(\xi)\geq m>0. l:L2​(Ω)→ℝl:L^{2}(\Omega)\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is a continuous linear form.
For the last several decades, various types of equations have been employed as some mathematical model describing physical, chemical, biological and ecological systems. Among them, the most successful and crucial one is the following model of semilinear parabolic partial differential equation, called the reaction-diffusion system

∂u∂t−D​Δ​u−f⁡(u)=0,\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}-D\,\Delta u-f(u)=0, (1.6)

where f:ℝn→ℝnf:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n} is a nonlinear function, and DD is an n×nn\times n real matrix of diffusion. This reaction-diffusion model is obtained by combining the system of nonlinear ordinary differential equations called the reaction system

d​ud​t−f⁡(u)=0,\displaystyle\frac{du}{dt}-f(u)=0, (1.7)

and the system of linear partial differential equation called the diffusion system

∂u∂t−D​Δ​u=0.\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}-D\,\Delta u=0. (1.8)

In 1998, L. A. F. Oliveira [12] considered the reaction-diffusion system where DD was a n×nn\times n real matrix and f:ℝn→ℝnf:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n} is a C2C^{2} function. He studied the exponential decay for some cases. Except for some publications on the subject, such as the searching for traveling waves solutions and some problem in ecology and epidemic theory, most of authors assume that diffusion matrix DD is diagonal, so that the coupling between the equations are present only on the nonlinearity of the reaction term f.f. However, cross-diffusion phenomena are not uncommon (see [4] and references therein) can be treated as equations like in which DD is not even diagonalizable. In 1997, M. Chipot and B. Lovat [5] studied the existence and uniqueness of the solutions for non local problems

ut−a⁡(∫Ωu⁡(x,t)​𝑑x)​Δ​u\displaystyle u_{t}-a\left(\int_{\Omega}u(x,\,t)\,dx\right)\Delta u =\displaystyle= f⁡(x,t)inΩ×(0,T)\displaystyle f(x,\,t)\quad\mbox{in}\quad\Omega\times(0,\,T) (1.9)
u⁡(x,t)\displaystyle u(x,\,t) =\displaystyle= 0on∂Ω×(0,T)\displaystyle 0\quad\mbox{on}\quad\partial\Omega\times(0,\,T) (1.10)
u⁡(x, 0)\displaystyle u(x,\,0) =\displaystyle= u0​(x)onΩ\displaystyle u_{0}(x)\quad\mbox{on}\quad\Omega (1.11)

where Ω\Omega is a bounded open subset in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} n≥1n\geq 1 with smooth boundary ∂Ω.\partial\Omega. TT is some arbitrary time. aa is some function from ℝ\mathbb{R} into (0,+∞).(0,\,+\infty). This problem arises in various situations, for instance uu could describe the density of a population(for instance of bacteria) subject to spreading. The diffusion coefficient aa is then supposed to depend on the entire population in the domain rather than on the local density i. e. moves are guided by considering the global state of the medium. They proven the following result:

Theorem 1.1. Let T0>0,T_{0}>0, u0∈L2​(Ω),u_{0}\in L^{2}(\Omega), u0≥0,u_{0}\geq 0, u0≢0.u_{0}\not\equiv 0. Let aa be a continuous function positive in a neighborhood of ∫Ωu0​𝑑x.\int_{\Omega}u_{0}\,dx. Then for f∈L2​([0,T]:H−1​(Ω))f\in L^{2}([0,\,T]:\,H^{-1}(\Omega)) there exists 0<T≤T00<T\leq T_{0} and uu solution to (1.9)-(1.11) such that

u∈L2​([0,T]:H01​(Ω))∩C0​([0,T]:L2​(Ω)),\displaystyle u\in L^{2}([0,\,T]:\,H_{0}^{1}(\Omega))\cap C^{0}([0,\,T]:\,L^{2}(\Omega)),
ut∈L2​([0,T]:H−1​(Ω)),\displaystyle u_{t}\in L^{2}([0,\,T]:\,H^{-1}(\Omega)),
<ut,v>+a⁡(∫Ωu​𝑑x)​(∇u⋅∇v)=<f,v>∀v∈H01​(Ω),a.e.t∈[0,T0]\displaystyle<u_{t},\,v>+\;a\left(\int_{\Omega}u\,dx\right)(\nabla u\cdot\nabla v)=<f,\,v>\quad\forall\;v\in H_{0}^{1}(\Omega),\quad a.\,e.\quad t\in[0,\,T_{0}]

where (∇u⋅∇v)=∫Ω∇u⋅∇v​𝑑x.(\nabla u\cdot\nabla v)=\int_{\Omega}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\,dx.

In 2005, S. D. Menezes [7], give a simple extension of the result obtained by M. Chipot and B. Lovat [5], considering a=a⁡(l⁡(u)),a=a(l(u)), f=f⁡(u)f=f(u) continuous functions. Indeed, they studied the existence, uniqueness and periodic solution for the following parabolic problem

ut−a⁡(l⁡(u))​Δ​u+f⁡(u)\displaystyle u_{t}-a(l(u))\Delta u+f(u) =\displaystyle= hinΩ×(0,T)\displaystyle h\quad\mbox{in}\quad\Omega\times(0,\,T) (1.12)
u⁡(x,t)\displaystyle u(x,\,t) =\displaystyle= 0on∂Ω×(0,T)\displaystyle 0\quad\mbox{on}\quad\partial\Omega\times(0,\,T) (1.13)
u⁡(x, 0)\displaystyle u(x,\,0) =\displaystyle= u0​(x)onΩ\displaystyle u_{0}(x)\quad\mbox{on}\quad\Omega (1.14)

where Ω\Omega is a bounded open subset in ℝn,\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥1n\geq 1 with smooth boundary ∂Ω.\partial\Omega. TT is some arbitrary time. l:L2​(Ω)→ℝl:L^{2}(\Omega)\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is a nonlinear form, h∈L2(0,T:H−1(Ω))h\in L^{2}(0,\,T:\,H^{-1}(\Omega)) and T>0T>0 is some fixed time. This problem is nonlocal in the sense that the diffusion coefficient is determined by a global quantity. This kind of problems, besides its mathematical motivation because of presence of the nonlocal term a⁡(l⁡(u)),a(l(u)), arises from physical situations related to migration of a population of bacteria in a container in which the velocity of migration ν→=a∇u\overrightarrow{\nu}=a\,\nabla u depends on the global population in a subdomain Ω′⊂Ω\Omega^{\prime}\subset\Omega given by a=a⁡(∫Ω′u​𝑑x).a=a(\int_{\Omega^{\prime}}u\,dx). For more information [5] and reference therein.

This article is concerned with to prove the existence, uniqueness and the exponential decay of the system (1.1)-(1.5) using the energy method. The method of energy consists of to use appropriate multipliers to build a functional of Lyapunov, in this direction we prove that for this types of materials where the energy, that can flow from one part to another, is strong enough to produce exponential decay for the solution of the coupled system.

This paper is organized as follows. Before the main result, in section 2 we briefly outline the notation and terminology to be used subsequently. In the section three we prove the existence and uniqueness of solution, in the section four we prove the exponential decay of solution of the system. Finally, numerical evidence corroborating our theoretical results is given in section five. In this paper, we prove the following two theorem:

Theorem 1.2. Let (u0,v0)∈L2​(Ω)×L2​(Ω)(u_{0},\,v_{0})\in L^{2}(\Omega)\times L^{2}(\Omega) and 0<T<+∞,0<T<+\infty, where the time TT depends only |u0|L2​(Ω)|u_{0}|_{L^{2}(\Omega)} and |v0|L2​(Ω).|v_{0}|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}. If (2.6)-(2.9) holds, then there is at most one solution of (1.1)-(1.5) in L2(0,T:H01(Ω))∩C([0,T):L2(Ω))×L2(0,T:H01(Ω))∩C([0,T):L2(Ω))L^{2}(0,\,T:\,H_{0}^{1}(\Omega))\cap C([0,\,T):\,L^{2}(\Omega))\times L^{2}(0,\,T:\,H_{0}^{1}(\Omega))\cap C([0,\,T):\,L^{2}(\Omega)) with initial data (u⁡(x, 0),v⁡(x, 0))=(u0,v0).(u(x,\,0),\,v(x,\,0))=(u_{0},\,v_{0}).

Theorem 1.3. Let (u,v)(u,\,v) be a solution of system (1.1)-(1.5) given by the theorem 1.2, then there exist positives constants CC and η,\eta, such that

E⁡(t)≤C​E​(0)​e−η​t.\displaystyle E(t)\leq C\,E(0)\,e^{-\eta\,t}. (1.15)

3 Existence and Uniqueness of a local solution

vt−a⁡(l⁡(v))​Δ​v\displaystyle v_{t}-a(l(v))\,\Delta v =\displaystyle= f⁡(u,v)−g⁡(u,v)inQ=Ω×(0,T)\displaystyle f(u,\,v)-g(u,\,v)\quad\mbox{in}\quad Q=\Omega\times(0,\,T) (3.2)

where we denote f⁡(u,v)≡f⁡(u−v)f(u,\,v)\equiv f(u-v) and g⁡(u,v)≡α⁡(u−v).g(u,\,v)\equiv\alpha\,(u-v).

4 Exponential stability

In this section we show that the total energy (2.11) associated to system (2.1)-(2.5) decay exponentially to zero as tt tends to infinity. In what follows we will prove our main result:

Theorem 4.1. Let (u,v)(u,\,v) be a solution of system (1.1)-(1.5) given by the theorem 3.1 and theorem 3.2. We suppose that m>2​cp​(M1+α)>0m>2\,c_{p}\,(M_{1}+\alpha)>0, where cpc_{p} corresponds to the constant of the Poincaré inequality.. Then there exist positives constants CC and η,\eta, such that

E⁡(t)≤C​E​(0)​e−η​t.\displaystyle E(t)\leq C\,E(0)\,e^{-\eta\,t}. (4.1)

Proof. Multiplying equation (2.1) by uu and integrating over x∈Ωx\in\Omega we have

12dd​t∫Ω|u|2dx+a(ℓ(u))∫Ω|∇u|2dx=−∫Ωf(u−v)udx+α∫Ω(u−v)udx.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}|u|^{2}\,dx+a(\ell(u))\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\,dx=-\int_{\Omega}f(u-v)\,u\,dx+\alpha\int_{\Omega}(u-v)\,u\,dx.

Multiplying equation (2.2) by vv and integrating over x∈Ωx\in\Omega we have

12​dd​t​∫Ω|v|2​𝑑x+a⁡(ℓ⁡(v))​∫Ω|∇v|2​𝑑x=∫Ωf⁡(u−v)​v​𝑑x−α​∫Ω(u−v)​v​𝑑x.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}|v|^{2}\,dx+a(\ell(v))\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{2}\,dx=\int_{\Omega}f(u-v)\,v\,dx-\alpha\int_{\Omega}(u-v)\,v\,dx.

Adding the expressions above and using (2.8) we have

12​dd​t​∫Ω[|u|2+|v|2]​𝑑x+m​∫Ω[|∇u|2+|∇v|2]​𝑑x≤∫Ω|f⁡(u−v)||u−v|𝑑x+α​∫Ω|u−v|2​𝑑x.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}\left[\,|u|^{2}+|v|^{2}\,\right]dx+m\int_{\Omega}\left[\,|\nabla u|^{2}+|\nabla v|^{2}\,\right]dx\leq\int_{\Omega}|f(u-v)|\;|u-v|\,dx+\alpha\int_{\Omega}|u-v|^{2}\,dx.

Using (2.6) follows that

dd​tE(t)≤−m∫Ω[|∇u|2+|∇v|2]dx+(M1+α)∫Ω|u−v|2dx.\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}E(t)\leq-m\int_{\Omega}\left[\,|\nabla u|^{2}+|\nabla v|^{2}\,\right]\,dx+(M_{1}+\alpha)\int_{\Omega}|u-v|^{2}\,dx.

Applying the Poincaré inequality and the Young inequality, we obtain

dd​t​E​(t)≤−2​mcp​E​(t)+4​(M1+α)​E​(t).\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}E(t)\leq-\frac{2m}{c_{p}}\,E(t)+4\,(M_{1}+\alpha)\,E(t).

Now choosing m>2​cp​(M1+α)>0m>2\,c_{p}\,(M_{1}+\alpha)>0 follows that there exists C>0C>0 such that

dd​t​E​(t)≤−C​E​(t).\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}E(t)\leq-\,C\,E(t).

From we concludes that there exists η>0\eta>0 such that

E⁡(t)≤C​E​(0)​e−η​t.\displaystyle E(t)\leq\,C\,E(0)\,e^{-\eta\,t}.

The proof follows.

5 Numerical Results

In this section we consider a particular case of the nonlocal reaction diffusion equations (2.1)-(2.5) in one dimensional space (n=1n=1), Ω=(0,1)\Omega=(0,1), and l:L2​(Ω)→ℝl:L^{2}(\Omega)\rightarrow\mathbb{R} defined by l⁡(u)=∫01u⁡(x)​𝑑xl(u)=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}u(x)dx. Then we approximate the solution of the system using implicit finite differences. The numerical scheme reads as following

uik+1−uikδ​x−a⁡(∑j=1Jδ​x​ujk)​ui+1k+1−2​uik+1+ui−1k+1δ​x2+f⁡(uik−vik)=α⁡(uik−vik),\displaystyle\frac{u^{k+1}_{i}-u^{k}_{i}}{\delta x}-a\left({\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{J}\delta xu^{k}_{j}}\right)\frac{u^{k+1}_{i+1}-2u^{k+1}_{i}+u^{k+1}_{i-1}}{\delta x^{2}}+f(u^{k}_{i}-v^{k}_{i})=\alpha(u^{k}_{i}-v^{k}_{i}), (5.1)
vik+1−vikδ​x−a⁡(∑j=1Jδ​x​vjk)​vi+1k+1−2​vik+1+vi−1k+1δ​x2−f⁡(uik−vik)=α⁡(vik−uik),\displaystyle\frac{v^{k+1}_{i}-v^{k}_{i}}{\delta x}-a\left({\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{J}\delta xv^{k}_{j}}\right)\frac{v^{k+1}_{i+1}-2v^{k+1}_{i}+v^{k+1}_{i-1}}{\delta x^{2}}-f(u^{k}_{i}-v^{k}_{i})=\alpha(v^{k}_{i}-u^{k}_{i}), (5.2)
u0k+1=uJk+1=v0k+1=vJk+1=0\displaystyle u^{k+1}_{0}=u^{k+1}_{J}=v^{k+1}_{0}=v^{k+1}_{J}=0 (5.3)

for i=1,…,J−1i=1,\ldots,J-1 and k=0,…,Kk=0,\ldots,K, where δ​t=T/K\delta t=T/K, δ​x=1/J\delta x=1/J, xi=i​δ​xx_{i}=i\delta x, i=0,…,Ji=0,\ldots,J and tk=k​δ​tt_{k}=k\delta t, k=0,…,Kk=0,\ldots,K. In (5.1)-(5.3), uiku^{k}_{i} denotes the approximation of u⁡(tk,xi)u(t_{k},x_{i}). In order to solve the system (5.1)-(5.3), we consider the initial condition approximated by

ui0=u0​(xi), and vi0=v0​(xi),for ​i=0,…,J.\displaystyle u^{0}_{i}=u_{0}(x_{i}),\quad\hbox{ and }\quad v^{0}_{i}=v_{0}(x_{i}),\qquad\hbox{for }i=0,\ldots,J. (5.4)

For each k=0,…,Kk=0,\ldots,K, the scheme (5.1)-(5.3) is equivalent to a linear system with a tridiagonal matrix of ℝ(J−1)×(J−1)\mathbb{R}^{(J-1)\times(J-1)} which is positive definited and then there exists a unique solution of (5.1)-(5.4).

In order to compare the numerical behaviour of the solution with theoretical and numerical behaviour of the solution for one equation (scalar case), we take the same nonlinear reaction terms with similar parameters and initial conditions of Ackle and Ke [2]. Nonlinear reaction and nonlocal diffusion are given by

a⁡(ξ)\displaystyle a(\xi) :⁣=\displaystyle:= max⁡{ε,1|ξ|}+m0,for all ​ξ,\displaystyle\max\left\{\varepsilon,\dfrac{1}{\left|\xi\right|}\right\}+m_{0},\qquad\hbox{for all }\xi, (5.5)
f⁡(w)−α​w\displaystyle f(w)-\alpha w :⁣=\displaystyle:= r​w​(κ−w),for all ​w,\displaystyle rw(\kappa-w),\qquad\hbox{for all }w, (5.6)

where ε\varepsilon, m0m_{0}, rr and κ\kappa are constant and positive parameters. We remark that in the numerical example of Ackle and Ke [2], the authors consider a nonlocal diffusion given by the expression 1∫01u⁡(x)​𝑑x\dfrac{1}{\int_{0}^{1}u(x)dx}. In our case the parameter ε\varepsilon is a very small parameter and it plays a practical computational role to avoid the numerical overflow on the diffusion when the extinction of the population occurs, that is when u≈0u\approx 0 or v≈0v\approx 0. We consider a parameter m0m_{0} to the numerical study of an extinsion case of population and for a persistence case of population. In fact, the exponential decaying of the energy (4.1), can be interpreted as the extinsion of two populations uu and vv. That is occurs when the hypothesis m>cp​(M1+α)m>c_{p}(M_{1}+\alpha) of the Theorem 4.1, is verified. If mm is too small, the decaying of the energy is not guarantee and a population persistence can be occur as we see in Figure 2.

The initial condition is given by u0​(x)=δ​sin⁡(π​x)u_{0}(x)=\delta\sin(\pi x), with δ=1.95\delta=1.95 (see [2]), and v0​(x)=−u0​(x)=−δ​sin⁡(π​x)v_{0}(x)=-u_{0}(x)=-\delta\sin(\pi x). In this example, a negative v0v_{0} has not a physical or biological sense, if uu and vv represent densities of population, but we want to focus in the importance of the hypothesis of the Theorem 4.1, showing numerically that the exponential decaying of the energy does no occur when the hypothesis is not verified. We choose the parameter ε=10−6\varepsilon=10^{-6} for the nonlocal diffusion function (5.5), and we choose r=1.0r=1.0 and k=10.0k=10.0 for the reaction function (5.6). The discretization is given by J=104J=10^{4} and K=104K=10^{4}; we solve the linear system (5.1)-(5.3) using Thomas algorithm programming in Fortran90.

We consider here 2 simulations, the first one with m0=1.0m_{0}=1.0 (see Figure 1), and the second one with m0=0.1m_{0}=0.1 (see Figure 2). The population persistence phenomenom does not occur with a choice of a big amplitude δ\delta for the initial condition as it occurs in [2]. In fact we made simulations with different δ\delta values and the exponential decaying is always observed.
